teaser.text: NetApp sells the systems and software that keep an organization’s data available, protected and usable. Its dollar comes from selling storage, supporting it over time, and increasingly delivering it through subscriptions and cloud partnerships.

blocks.heading: Where could NetApp's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast puts NetApp below today’s price at all three dates. At October 2027, the weighted price is $161.87, down 20% including dividends. At October 2028, it is $167.90, down 16%. At October 2029, it is $180.15, down 9%.
The forecast assigns 30% to the bear case, 50% to the base case and 20% to the bull case, making steady execution the most likely path.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for NetApp, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: Earnings are the largest difference between the scenarios. The base case rises from $1,550 million in October 2027 to $1,690 million in October 2028 and $1,840 million in October 2029. It assumes revenue and margins improve steadily without a major AI windfall. The starting point is close to the FY2027 GAAP outlook of $7.35–$7.65 EPS and $7.975–$8.225 billion of revenue.

The bull case requires flash share gains to persist, AI pilots to become paid production deployments and cloud and Keystone growth to produce repeatable cash returns. Pricing offsets component inflation, buybacks approach the remaining authorization and investors sustain a premium multiple. The result is $221.12 initially and $339.07 by October 2029. Its 20% probability reflects the strength of recent flash and cloud growth, but the absence of demonstrated repeat AI economics keeps it below the base case.

blocks.heading: How much cash does NetApp really make?

paragraphs.text: Stock compensation explains part of the difference. NetApp recorded $382 million of share-based pay in FY2026 and added it back in cash flow because issuing shares uses no immediate cash. Employees still receive something valuable, so treating that amount as entirely free cash would ignore dilution. Deducting it produces the “real free cash flow” convention used here.

blocks.heading: Is NetApp's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left from operations after purchases of property and equipment. Research and development is already included in operating expenses, so the measure reflects cash after funding the people and software that drive the business. NetApp generated substantial free cash flow over the five fiscal years ending in April 2026, and distributions were slightly below it.

FY2026 operating cash flow was $2,067 million, above net income of $1,276 million. After $198 million of capital spending, free cash flow was $1,869 million. Capital spending is not the whole cost of competitiveness because engineering and product development also run through operating expenses.

The forecast keeps increases modest because free cash flow recently fell to $401 million from $620 million, while dividends and repurchases compete for cash.

blocks.heading: What is NetApp's dividend yield at today's price?

paragraphs.text: Cash flow gives a more practical test of the valuation. FY2026 free cash flow was $1,869 million, compared with $1,338 million in FY2025, but faster collections and other working-capital movements helped. The reported 4.7% free-cash-flow yield therefore deserves comparison with the 3.7% “real” yield after adjustment. Buybacks can also lift EPS without lifting total profit: diluted shares fell from 206 million to 199 million in Q4 FY2026. The dividend yield is 1.0%.

blocks.heading: Did NetApp keep its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Management has also delivered against financial guidance. Its FY26 fourth-quarter presentation showed revenue and adjusted earnings per share above earlier ranges. On September 2, 2026, Kurian and Jabre reported another quarter above guidance while acknowledging help from an extra week, accelerated purchases, and pricing benefits.

blocks.heading: What is NetApp's eight-quarter revenue and profit trend?

paragraphs.text: The eight-quarter sequence suggests the acceleration began before July. The test now is whether sales continue after the calendar benefit disappears, inventory converts into shipments and cash, and product margins withstand component costs.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in NetApp's next results?

paragraphs.text: The first dated test is December 1, 2026, when NetApp targets its Q2 results. Investors should compare revenue and margins with the September promises, then ask whether later orders confirm demand or reveal a gap caused by purchases brought forward.

The income statement should separate equipment, support, public cloud and subscription storage. Gross margin measures direct economics; operating margin includes research, sales and administration; net margin includes interest and tax. EPS must be read alongside diluted shares, because buybacks can lift EPS without lifting total profit.
